newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia passes controversial nuclear energy law.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia passes controversial nuclear energy law.

text.p: Indonesia's parliament approved a controversial nuclear energy law on Wednesday amid concerns from anti-nuclear activists that the bill did not address key issues of nuclear safety.

"I hope we never have to build a nuclear power station," Research and Technology Minister Jusuf Habibie said outside the parliament. "Nuclear power stations are the last alternative, but when the time comes that we need nuclear power we cannot avoid it," he said.

Agencies under Habibie's control have, however, been pushing for the country's first nuclear power plant to be built in central Java starting in 1998 or 1999, pending the results of a feasibility study of the project.

The passing of the bill into law was also attacked by a member of one minority party because it was processed by a near empty chamber of Indonesia's mostly rubber stamp parliament in an apparent contravention of the body's own rules.
Habibie, representing the government at the session, later told reporters the new law was not meant to legalise the construction of nuclear power stations but update a 1964 atomic energy law.

An Indonesian atomic energy official said in Darwin on Monday that the proposed power plant would have a capacity to generate 7,200 megawatts by 2015 and consume between 120 and 180 tonnes of uranium a year.
The official said American, Japanese, South Korean and Canadian interests are all studying the proposal to build the plant on a build/own/operate basis.

Activists have attacked the plan to build the nuclear power plant on the slopes of Mount Muria, an extinct volcano, because the proposed site is said to be in an earthquake-prone area of Java, home to about 60 percent of Indonesia's 200 million people.

On Wednesday, Indonesian Democratic Party legislator Meri Laksmiari Priyonggo walked out of parliament in protest because she said a quorom was not present as only about 60 of the body's 500 members were there. A quorom consists of 250 legislators.

Outside the parliament, 50 members of the Indonesian Anti- Nuclear Society (MANI) staged a peaceful protest against the bill which they said was designed to ensure a nuclear power station would be built without public consultation.

MANI said the new law made no reference to the country's existing laws on environmental protection, electricity generation or industry as well as ignoring regulations of the International Atomic Energy Agency and other international agreements.
